Bowen 1947-2026 August 7, 2026 Trending NEW MIDDLETOWN -- Wayne L. Bowen, 78, entered into eternal rest on Friday, July 31, 2026, surrounded by the love of his family. Born on Dec. 18, 1947, in Greenville, Pa., Wayne was the beloved son of the late Richard and Mary Zuschlag Bowen. A 1965 graduate of Greenville High School, Wayne proudly served in the United States Army from 1966 to 1969, including service in Vietnam. He was honorably discharged as a Specialist 5 E-5 and received several military decorations, highlighted by the Army Commendation Medal for meritorious service. On Jan. 29, 1972, Wayne married Andrea Glista; and together they shared more than 55 years of marriage built on love, loyalty and unwavering devotion. Even as his own health declined, Wayne's greatest concern remained Andrea. Until his final day, he continued to put her needs before his own, while Andrea faithfully remained by his side. Following his military service, Wayne pursued engineering studies at Youngstown State University before beginning a 37-year career as a mechanic with Norfolk Southern Railway. He was known for his exceptional work ethic, remarkable mechanical ability and willingness to help others. He took great pride in passing those skills and values on to his children. Wayne enjoyed the outdoors, traveling, solving puzzles and spending time with those he loved. Above all, he was a devoted husband, father and extraordinarily proud grandfather. Wayne is survived by his beloved wife, Andrea; his four children, Patrick (Tracey) Bowen of San Diego, California, Matthew (Carla) Bowen of Canfield, Natalie (Tim) Pappagallo of Mineral Ridge and Richard (Jen) Bowen of Hudson; his nine cherished grandchildren, Olivia, Bryce, Madison, Morgan, Mason, Timmy, Dominic, Cameron and Ryan; his sister, Maxine (John) Hamilton of Farmington, Arkansas; his brothers- and sisters-in-law; and many beloved nieces, nephews, extended family members and dear friends. Wayne's life was defined by faithfulness to his country, his family and an honest day's work. His humility, generosity and quiet example of service will continue to guide his family for generations to come. Family and friends may pay their respects from 9 to 11 a.m. Monday, Aug. 10, 2026, at Higgins Reardon Funeral Homes, Poland Chapel. A prayer service will immediately follow calling hours, beginning at 11 a.m. at the funeral home. Family and friends are invited to then travel in procession to Calvary Cemetery, where he will be laid to rest with military honors. (special notice) Starting at /week. Subscribe Today

https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-bur.text: LONDON — Britain’s new prime minister spent his first statement to parliament promising to “bring back hope.” Over 204 minutes he demonstrated just how many of those hopes could ultimately be dashed. Taking 125 questions in the Commons Tuesday, Andy Burnham made, hardened or reiterated a dizzying flurry of commitments that would radically alter the British state — if he manages to see them all through. The man who became PM just 43 days ago suggested he will scrap Britain’s first-past-the-post voting system before 2034 if a majority of parties pledging reform — such his own Labour Party plus the centrist Liberal Democrats — win “consensus” at the next general election, due by 2029. He hinted that he could cap individual U.K. donations to political parties or block those from abroad entirely in future (though as POLITICO revealed, he has declined to do either in the short term ). Advertisement Advertisement He pledged to shake up England’s privatized water sector as part of a “10-year plan” this fall. He promised to impose his predecessor Keir Starmer’s social media ban on under-16s “at pace.” He repeated his long-held vows to radically reform the social care system, move powers and officials out of Whitehall, release public land for a wave of house-building and “end” rough sleeping — while still bringing down the welfare bill. “Working together to build a new sense of optimism around the country, we can make this next decade better than the last,” he said. The parliamentary chamber began to empty, MPs turning to other duties and their bladders, as the hardiest stayed behind in the hope they would extract yet another commitment from the prime minister. As the session wore on, Burnham hinted he could one day scrap England’s system of local taxation, which is based on property valuations from 1991. In the third hour he even promised to save Jodrell Bank, a locally-beloved cluster of deep space radio telescopes near Manchester that has had its funding cut. The new prime minister was not offering a free-for-all and, like any minister, swerved more invitations to commit policy than he accepted. He insisted he will make tough choices. Yet he is also enjoying a practical by-effect of being a new leader: He hasn’t yet had to disappoint all the people he will eventually disappoint. Rhetoric vs. reality The 125 questions he took showed that the difficulties and trade-offs that come with power are already coming into view. Advertisement Advertisement Burnham dropped a hint that he could raise defense spending to 3 percent of GDP by 2030 — a key demand of his chief finance minister, John Healey, when he quit Starmer’s government earlier this year as defense minister. Burnham said he had appointed Healey “precisely because” of his arguments on defense. Yet both men have pushed back any decision to a spending review in 2027, and will not face easy choices; the U.K.’s long-term borrowing costs are their highest since 1998, and Burnham declined to rule out tax rises in Healey’s fall budget. On paper, the position did not move on Tuesday. The tension was summed up in Burnham’s promise to bring “much more substantial change as promised in [our] 2024 manifesto.” Healey last week put the same thing very differently, saying it was a “continuity of a Labour government with a change of leader.” Contradictions are already emerging within Burnham’s approach. The new prime minister wants to keep his focus more domestic than Starmer’s, but said he will head to the COP31 climate summit this November . He also promised a statement “very shortly” responding to Israel’s E1 settlement project in the West Bank, which he said “could imperil, if not end, the two-state solution.” That statement will strain relations with Israel and could do so too with Donald Trump, who Burnham is hoping to meet on a U.S. trip in late September. He said the recent mass fatalities in Nepal, caused by falling glacier ice, were “what the climate crisis looks like.” But with energy prices rising, Burnham hinted his government will soon approve at least one of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas projects in the North Sea. Advertisement Advertisement Not even the Commons theatrics were immune. Moments after he pledged to avoid point-scoring, Burnham pointed some jabs at the 49-day premiership of former Tory PM Liz Truss. Past is precedent Elsewhere, Burnham’s promises to change the way things are done in Britain are butting up against reasons why they were done that way in the first place. The PM told MPs that Brexit had inflicted “a decade of low growth” and promised to get closer to Brussels ahead of an EU-U.K. summit in the fall. Yet like his predecessor he will be bound simultaneously by the EU’s red lines and his own. Burnham has chosen to continue Labour’s 2024 pledge not to rejoin the single market or customs union. He appeared tearful when he promised to invest “all” his political capital into reforming the social care model, but even that cannot happen fast thanks to the complexity of the system; his intervention has been to bring forward a review from 2028 to 2027. He promised to be “relentless” in bringing in more “public control” of the water industry, but as POLITICO reported, his officials are still wading through all the ownership models and could apply several at the same time. He left the door open to banning all overseas donations to U.K. political parties (saying “we can come back to these issues” before 2029), and to imposing a cap on individual donations (“we do need to go further,” he added). But unions worry their donations to Labour would be imperiled by a cap, and Burnham punted any action to an ongoing taskforce on democracy rather than accepting amendments to a bill this week. Advertisement Advertisement He also left the door open to reforming the council tax system, but made clear that he already knows the danger in expending too much political capital. (When Conservative PM Margaret Thatcher last tried major reforms in 1990, there were riots in the streets; the successor system dating to 1991 has remained ever since.) “I don’t think I can go all that way today [… but] a council tax system based on 1991 valuations is not going to deliver fairness across the country,” he said. “We need to proceed with consensus if we can.” Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of presiding over “a government swerving all over the place” that is obsessed with Thatcher’s legacy of privatization. “He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s,” she said. For many of his own Labour MPs, Burnham is saying what they want to hear — at least for now. “The grasp of detail is impressive,” said one, granted anonymity to speak candidly. The statement was “good,” said another. (The adulation is not universal; a third Labour MP confessed: “I’ll be honest, I was doing emails and forgot.”) But as Starmer retreats from parliament — the former PM announced Tuesday that he will stand down from the Commons entirely — MPs are turning their full focus to his successor. At some point, they and the public will expect the many promises to be fulfilled. The question is when they decide that point has arrived.

https://www.omanobserver.om/article/1194.text: Built during the Middle Ages to shelter communities from attacks, Transylvania’s fortified churches risk crumbling despite efforts to preserve them and breathe new life into the buildings.In a stark reminder of their fragility, part of the outer wall of a historic church in Mosna, central Romania — visited by Britain’s King Charles III in 1998 — collapsed one night in June.Since then, Mariana Rempler, the village’s last remaining woman from the German-speaking Saxon minority, has feared that one of the church’s towers could also collapse. The site attracts around 4,000 visitors a year.“I felt a great pain inside me. It was as if I had collapsed at the same time with that wall”, the 74-year-old said, recalling the incident with tears in her eyes inside the church where she was baptised and married. Mosna is home to one of more than 160 fortified churches in Transylvania. Surrounded by defensive walls, they were built by the German minority to shelter people from attacks by Tatars and Ottomans in what was then a disputed border territory.As the Saxons left Romania — many fleeing the communist dictatorship of Nicolae Ceausescu — several churches deteriorated, with no one remaining to care for them.Even sites such as Mosna, renovated after the fall of communism in 1989, remain at risk as funding for further work is difficult to secure.Of the approximately 300,000 Saxons who lived in Transylvania before World War II, only around 10,000 remain today. About half of the region’s fortified churches — around 80, including Mosna — have undergone restoration during the past 35 years or are expected to do so over the next five, according to Cristian Cismaru, manager of the Fortified Churches Foundation.The foundation works with the Evangelical Church in Romania to preserve the monuments through grants and donations, with around 85 per cent of its funding coming from the European Union.“I don’t think we’ll be able to address the other half of our heritage in our lifetime. That will be left for future generations”, Cismaru said. “Our role, those of us who live in Transylvania, regardless of nationality, race or religion, is to continue to look after these monuments”, he said. “We want to breathe new life into these fortified churches”.Cismaru said many churches need “a new concept for their survival” because they can no longer function solely as places of worship. One proposal is to transform them into cultural spaces.Earlier this month, the churches hosted dozens of events as part of Romania’s largest annual festival promoting Saxon heritage. It drew a record of almost 10,000 visitors this year, according to organisers. In Mosna, Mayor Dumitru Nutu said more tourists have come to see the church since the wall collapsed.“I keep seeing them from the town hall window. They’re all taking photos of the broken wall”, Nutu said.Hundreds of scattered bricks, covered by a plastic sheet, are piled at the foot of the endangered tower, which was propped up with wooden beams in 2017.Like the tourists, Rempler photographs the tower daily to document its visible cracks and encourage action.“I’m afraid that in a month or two, that tower won’t still be standing”, she said, fearing the structure could collapse without the wall to support it.She hopes the collapse will serve as a wake-up call and that a solution will be found.“It would be a shame for us to let it fall into ruin”. — AFP

In brief: Kyiv may need more Western aid, but its claim of a looming $27 billion budget shortfall doesn’t add up – and politics might explain why. By Euractiv Sept. 26, 2026, 3:34 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity Valdis Dombrovskis at the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, on Sept. 1, 2026. (Photo by Allison Joyce / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Journalists often make mistakes. As someone who dropped a bit of a clanger this week (I said there was a deal on the EU’s sanctions on Russian oligarchs 24 hours before there actually was one), I’m especially eager to avoid repeating one I made just a few months ago. Early this year I repeatedly wrote that Ukraine was set to run out of money in April, or – when I felt like being more specific – in “early” April. Nor was I alone: European Commission officials, Ukrainian officials, and many of my fellow journalists said the same thing. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . In retrospect, however, the claim never really made much sense. For one thing, it was never clear what it actually meant. (That Kyiv would default on its debt? If so, why not just say that? And if not, what?) For another, Ukraine’s behavior didn’t really fit that of a country that was on the brink of fiscal armageddon. Advertisement On Feb. 20, Hungary shocked Ukraine and its European allies when it announced that it would veto a €90 billion loan to Kyiv, citing the latter’s failure to restart oil flows through a damaged pipeline that transits Ukraine on its way from Russia to Hungary. Rather than dropping to its knees and begging Budapest to back down – or asking Brussels to break the impasse or (the most obvious solution) repairing the pipeline – Kyiv simply shrugged. “What’s the point of rebuilding [it]?” Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, said five days later. Other Topics of Interest Why the Baltics Are Right to Worry About Putin’s Latest Reassurances Putin denied plans to attack Europe but revived Russian-speaker grievances in the Baltics, echoing rhetoric Moscow used before invading Ukraine. For a country on the brink of bankruptcy, this was (to put it mildly) a very weird thing to say. But for a country that wasn’t, it wasn’t. As it later transpired, Ukraine wasn’t close to “running out of money,” at least in any meaningful sense. (Moreover, even if some kind of a fiscal crunch were imminent, Kyiv could have issued bonds to state banks or forced its central bank to print money to remain temporarily afloat.) Advertisement Ultimately, Kyiv’s actions were not driven by economics, but by politics. First, Ukraine was understandably reluctant to facilitate oil deliveries to a country (Hungary) whose pro-Moscow government had regularly sabotaged the EU’s Ukraine policy, and whose oil purchases would further enrich the country (Russia) that was attempting to destroy it. Second, and as Zelensky effectively admitted, blocking the crude transit was deemed an effective way of tilting Hungary’s parliamentary elections in mid-April in favor of Péter Magyar, the nemesis of then-premier Viktor Orbán. Magyar’s subsequent landslide victory suggests Zelensky was right. Not coincidentally, ten days after the elections, Kyiv finally allowed the oil to flow, causing Budapest to immediately lift its veto. Ukraine then spent the better part of two months haggling over the loan’s technical details with EU officials. Finally, on June 25, the first loan payout – €3.2 billion in budget support – was made. No other budget support from the loan has been disbursed since then (although €11.7 billion has been paid out for defense procurement). And, last time I checked, Ukraine still hasn’t run out of money. At least not yet. Advertisement Kyiv, give me a break! Why do I tell this story? In part, because I have a penchant for public self-flagellation. More importantly, though, I think recalling this history is crucial to understanding what’s happening today. Last month, Zelensky stunned his European allies when he announced that Ukraine faced a “budget shortfall” this year of $27 billion (€24 billion) – a sum equivalent to more than 10% of the country’s GDP. Once again, however, the claims don’t add up. Literally. According to Zelenskyy, “$8-10 billion” is required to buy “weapons and everything necessary” to ensure a “normal start” to next year, while “nearly $20 billion” is needed to pay soldiers’ salaries, the families of fallen soldiers, and “other areas of funding.” Zelensky has never defined what he means by “necessary”, “normal”, or “other areas of funding”. Nor has he explained how “$8-10 billion” + “nearly $20 billion” = $27 billion. (Why not, say, $28 billion? Or $29 billion? Or “nearly” $30 billion?) Tellingly, neither the European Commission nor the International Monetary Fund has been able to confirm Zelensky’s figures, despite weeks of intensive discussions. Even more tellingly, Brussels has resisted calls from some EU countries to plug the gap by accelerating payouts this year from the €90 billion loan – a clear sign that it doesn’t think any “shortfall” is imminent. Advertisement In an interview with me this week, Valdis Dombrovskis, the EU’s economy commissioner, strongly implied that Ukraine’s financing needs are less dire than Kyiv is suggesting. “By and large, [the] budgetary needs for Ukraine for this year seem to be broadly covered,” Dombrovskis said, adding that the country nevertheless requires additional military support. Kyiv’s demand for extra cash is especially puzzling when one recalls that so much funding for this year is still available. Maksym Samoiliuk, a senior economist at the Center for Economic Strategy, a Kyiv-based think tank, points out that around $29.5 billion in external financing (much of it from the EU) is currently being held up by the Ukrainian parliament’s failure to pass reforms. Why, then, demand more when you’re not taking what you can already get? Much like earlier this year, the key to this puzzle is to realize that politics, rather than economics, is driving Zelensky’s behavior. First, his demand plays well domestically. Calling for higher salaries for soldiers and bereaved families is always a sure-fire political winner. Asking foreigners to pay for this also exempts Zelenskyy from the awkward task of having to ask Ukrainians to pay for it themselves. Advertisement Second, it is aimed at Ukraine’s allies – in particular, it is intended to make Western governments, media, and citizens recognize (and ideally address) Ukraine’s increasingly dire economic situation. Mind the gap Viewed in this light, Zelensky’s actions are also perfectly reasonable. After all, Russia’s naval blockade of the Black Sea has starved Kyiv’s economy of export revenue from wheat and other goods in recent months. Moscow’s drone and missile strikes have also devastated Ukraine’s critical infrastructure and destroyed numerous tax revenue-generating businesses. Financial support from Europe’s allies, particularly the US, has also dried up. In other words, Ukraine does need help. But it can also help itself. As Dmytro Andriienko and Viktoriia Klimchuk of the Kyiv School of Economics have noted, Ukraine could seek to harness domestic sources of revenue, namely by cutting or postponing non-critical government expenditure and broadening its own tax base. By a happy coincidence, these latter measures are precisely among those demanded by the EU and the IMF. Advertisement Boosting domestic revenue, then, will help unlock foreign funding – a financial double blessing. Or as Dombrovskis put it: “When we are discussing additional funding gaps and possible additional funding sources, it [is] important that Ukraine actually uses the funding or receives the funding which is already available.” Ukraine’s failure to pass reforms, then, might prove to be the biggest mistake of all. It also risks being significantly more costly than mine – unless, of course, I’m very much mistaken. See this opinion piece for Euractiv by Thomas Moller-Nielsen here .
